title: The Conditional Operator
description: A one-line if and else that produces a value, and when not to use it.

parts.label: if true

parts.label: if false

content.title: Anatomy of a ternary
content.caption: Its official name is the **conditional operator**. People call it **ternary** because it takes three parts, where `+` takes two.

items.title: if and else
items.text: Fine, but long just to choose one word.

items.title: Ternary
items.text: Condition `?` value if true `:` value if false.

content.value: A ternary is an **expression**: it produces a value, so use it. `marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";` on its own line compiles, but the answer goes nowhere. Store it or print it.

content.question: What is stored in `r` when `age` is `12`?
content.explain: `12 >= 18` is false, so the value after the `:` is chosen.

content.value: A ternary shines inside a `cout`, where an `if` and `else` would need four extra lines to pick one word.

steps.note: `count == 1` is true, so it picks `" item"`.
`count == 1` is false, so it picks `" items"`.

content.title: Picking a word, picking a number
content.outro: The brackets round a ternary inside `cout` are required. `<<` is worked out before `?`, so without them the line does not compile.

content.caption: Any type works, numbers, `char`, `bool`, text, as long as both sides give the **same** kind of value. A number on one side and text on the other is a compile error.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `60 >= 75` is false, so the value after `:` is chosen.

items.sub: If the branches do real work, like several prints, use `if` and `else`.
A ternary inside a ternary is legal, and almost unreadable.

items.title: Nested ternary
items.text: Looks clever today. Costs ten minutes next week.

items.title: else if chain

content.title: The same grade rule, marks = 82
content.caption: Both give B. If you have to count the `?` and `:` symbols to read a line, it should have been an `if`.

content.question: You need to pick one of four messages. What fits best?
options: An else if chain or a switch
content.explain: A ternary chooses between exactly two values. Three or more alternatives belong in a chain or a switch.

content.title: Four ways to decide
content.caption: Each decision has its own shape, so each gets the tool that fits it.
The module project in miniature. When each case is one short assignment, the switch fits on one line per case. Change `age` and `day` and predict the output first.

content.question: With `age = 3` and `day = 6`, what is the second line?
content.explain: `3 < 5` makes the price 0, and the surcharge only applies when `price > 0`.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of the conditional operator, in order?
options: The condition, the value if true, the value if false
The value if true, the condition, the value if false
quiz.explain: `condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse`. The `?` separates the question from the answers and the `:` separates the two answers.

quiz.question: What does `int price = age < 13 ? 120 : 250;` store when age is 30?
quiz.explain: The condition is false for 30, so the value after the `:` is chosen.

quiz.question: What happens to `marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";` written on a line of its own?
options: It works out a value, but the value is thrown away, so nothing happens.
quiz.explain: The conditional operator produces a value and nothing more. Store it in a variable or send it to `cout` so the answer has somewhere to go.

quiz.question: Why do you need brackets in `cout << "Larger: " << (a > b ? a : b);`?
options: The conditional operator always requires brackets.
`<<` is worked out before `?`, so without them the line does not compile.
quiz.explain: `<<` binds more tightly than `>` and `?`, so C++ would try to send part of the condition to `cout` first. The brackets make the choice happen before printing.

quiz.question: When should you NOT use the conditional operator?
options: When the branches do real work, or when there are three or more alternatives
When choosing a word inside a cout
quiz.explain: It is for choosing one of two values. Work belongs in `if` and `else`, and several alternatives belong in a chain or a switch.
